title: Machine Learning Using Python
text:
About This Book
Machine Learning Using Python: Foundations, Algorithms, Applications, and Reproducible Research is designed for data enthusiasts, analysts, students, researchers, and professionals who want to develop a deeper understanding of machine learning using Python.
This Second Edition integrates conceptual foundations, mathematical reasoning, practical programming, real-world applications, responsible machine learning, and reproducible research.

title: Machine Learning Using Python
text:
Who This Book Is For
This book is intended for readers who want to move beyond simply fitting machine learning models toward understanding how algorithms work, how models should be evaluated, and how machine learning can be applied responsibly to meaningful real-world problems.

title: Machine Learning Using Python
text:
Second Edition
This edition substantially expands the first edition with greater emphasis on mathematical foundations, modern machine learning methods, hands-on practice, health and education applications, research design, reproducibility, and responsible artificial intelligence.

6.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
Explain the role of linear regression in predictive modeling.
Distinguish simple linear regression from multiple linear regression.
Interpret regression coefficients in context.
Explain the assumptions underlying ordinary least squares regression.
Derive and interpret common regression evaluation metrics.
Build a reproducible regression workflow in Python.

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.2 Why This Matters
Linear regression is one of the foundational algorithms in statistics and machine learning. Although modern machine learning includes highly complex models, linear regression remains valuable because it is interpretable, computationally efficient, and useful as a benchmark against which more complex models can be evaluated.

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.3 Real-World Problem
Suppose a public health researcher wants to predict systolic blood pressure using demographic, behavioral, and anthropometric characteristics.
Questions might include:

Which variables are most strongly associated with systolic blood pressure?
How accurately can blood pressure be predicted?
Does a more complex model substantially outperform linear regression?
Are prediction errors larger for some population subgroups than others?

Throughout this chapter, we will use problems like this to connect mathematical foundations with machine learning practice.

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.5 Mathematical Foundations

6.5.1 The Linear Regression Model
For a single predictor:
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i
\]
For multiple predictors:
\[
y_i =
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i1}
+
\beta_2x_{i2}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_px_{ip}
+
\epsilon_i
\]
where:

\(y_i\) is the observed outcome,
\(\beta_0\) is the intercept,
\(\beta_j\) represents the effect associated with predictor \(j\),
\(x_{ij}\) is the value of predictor \(j\) for observation \(i\),
\(\epsilon_i\) represents unexplained variation.



6.5.2 Ordinary Least Squares
The ordinary least squares estimator minimizes the residual sum of squares:
\[
RSS =
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
\]
In matrix notation:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y
\]


6.5.3 Loss Functions

6.5.3.1 Mean Squared Error
\[
MSE =
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
\]


6.5.3.2 Root Mean Squared Error
\[
RMSE =
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
}
\]


6.5.3.3 Mean Absolute Error
\[
MAE =
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
|y_i-\hat{y}_i|
\]


6.5.3.4 Coefficient of Determination
\[
R^2
=
1-
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\bar{y})^2
}
\]

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.15 Common Mistakes

Evaluating the model only on training data.
Interpreting association as causation.
Ignoring nonlinearity.
Performing preprocessing before separating training and test data.
Using \(R^2\) as the only evaluation metric.
Removing outliers without substantive justification.
Selecting predictors solely because they are statistically significant.

Why does strong predictive performance not establish causation?

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.18 Professor’s Challenge
A linear regression model produces:
\[
R^2 = 0.81
\]
on the training data but:
\[
R^2 = 0.54
\]
on the test data.
A colleague claims:

“The model explains 81% of the variation, so it is an excellent model.”

Critically evaluate this claim.
What additional evidence would you require before recommending the model for decision-making?

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.19 Research Extension
Transform the chapter case study into a potential research project.
Consider:

What is the substantive research gap?
What population is being studied?
Which predictors are theoretically justified?
What alternative algorithms should be benchmarked?
How will predictive uncertainty be evaluated?
Will model performance differ across demographic groups?
What contribution could make the study publishable?

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.20 Reproducibility Check
Before completing this chapter, verify that:

the analysis runs from beginning to end,
random seeds are documented,
data sources are cited,
preprocessing occurs inside the modeling workflow where appropriate,
the test set has not influenced model development,
software dependencies are documented.

title: 6  Linear Regression
text:
6.21 Key Takeaways

Linear regression remains an important baseline machine learning algorithm.
Prediction and statistical inference are related but distinct objectives.
Model evaluation should focus on unseen data.
Mathematical understanding helps identify when a model is inappropriate.
Reproducible workflows are essential for credible machine learning research.

Dimensionality reduction trades original-variable interpretability for compact representation.
PCA is grounded in variance and linear algebra.
Visualization embeddings require cautious interpretation.
